questions.stem: Under the World Heritage Convention, a natural site of 'outstanding universal value' is one that:
options: is owned jointly by every member country of the United Nations
is so significant it matters to all people, now and in future
earns the most tourism income for the country where it is located
has never been visited by any people at any time in its history
questions.explanation: Outstanding universal value means a place's significance transcends national boundaries and is important for present and future generations of all humanity. Sites remain under the sovereignty of their own country.

questions.stem: The Great Barrier Reef, inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1981, meets all four natural criteria. Which of these is one of those criteria?
options: containing important habitats for the conservation of biodiversity
containing the largest number of hotels of any natural environment
being located within 100 km of a nation's capital city
having been formed entirely by human activity over centuries
questions.explanation: The natural criteria cover superlative natural phenomena or beauty, major stages of Earth's history, significant ecological and biological processes, and important habitats for biodiversity.

questions.stem: A farmer, a surfer, a scientist and a tourist all describe a stretch of coast differently. This best illustrates that:
options: people's connection to nature varies with culture and experience
the natural world has exactly the same meaning and value for every person
only scientific measurements give a valid view of a natural environment
natural environments have no value unless they can be used for profit
questions.explanation: People connect with nature through work, recreation, culture, spirituality and knowledge, so the same place can hold different values for different groups. Geographers take these perspectives into account.

questions.stem: Describing a natural environment as a 'source of wonder' refers mainly to its:
options: aesthetic and inspirational value to people
market value as a source of raw materials
role as a dumping ground for urban waste
suitability for clearing and farming
questions.explanation: Landscapes such as canyons, reefs and mountains inspire awe and curiosity, an aesthetic and emotional value that is part of why environments are protected.

questions.stem: In systems thinking, a natural system such as a river catchment is described as an 'open system' because it:
options: contains no stores, only flows of water and sediment
exchanges both energy and matter with its surroundings
exchanges neither energy nor matter with its surroundings
receives energy from outside but never exchanges any matter
questions.explanation: A catchment receives inputs of rain and solar energy and loses water, sediment and heat as outputs. Earth as a whole is close to a closed system for matter but open for energy.

questions.stem: In a natural system, the ocean, ice sheets and groundwater are examples of:
options: flows
outputs
feedbacks
stores
questions.explanation: Stores (or reservoirs) hold matter or energy for a time, while flows or transfers, such as evaporation and runoff, move it between stores. Feedbacks are responses that amplify or dampen change.

questions.stem: Which factor most directly controls how much solar energy different parts of the Earth's surface receive?
options: longitude, which changes the time zone of a place
population density in each region
the age of the rocks at the surface
latitude, which changes the angle of the sun's rays
questions.explanation: Near the equator the sun's rays strike more directly, concentrating energy; towards the poles they arrive at a low angle and spread over a larger area. This imbalance drives atmospheric and ocean circulation.

questions.stem: The natural greenhouse effect warms the Earth because greenhouse gases in the atmosphere:
options: reflect incoming sunlight back into space before it reaches the surface
create holes in the ozone layer that let in more ultraviolet radiation
block all incoming solar radiation so that heat cannot escape at night
absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit some back to the surface
questions.explanation: The surface absorbs sunlight and emits infrared radiation; gases such as water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb some of it and radiate energy back down. Without this effect, Earth's average temperature would be well below freezing.

questions.stem: Surplus energy in the tropics and a deficit near the poles are balanced mainly by:
options: the movement of tectonic plates from the poles to the equator
the storage of all surplus tropical heat in the deep ocean
the reflection of extra tropical heat straight back into space
the transfer of heat poleward by winds and ocean currents
questions.explanation: Atmospheric circulation cells, weather systems and currents such as the East Australian Current move heat from low to high latitudes, linking the atmosphere and hydrosphere.

questions.stem: About what share of the Earth's water is salt water in the oceans?
options: about 30%
about 97%
about 50%
about 75%
questions.explanation: Around 97% of Earth's water is in the oceans. Of the small share that is fresh, most is locked in ice sheets and glaciers or stored as groundwater, with only a tiny fraction in rivers and lakes.

questions.stem: Most of the Earth's fresh water is stored in:
options: living plants and animals
ice sheets and glaciers
rivers and lakes
the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Ice sheets and glaciers hold roughly two-thirds of fresh water, and groundwater most of the rest. Rivers, lakes and the atmosphere hold very small amounts at any one time.

questions.stem: Water evaporated from the Coral Sea falls as rain on the Great Dividing Range and flows back to the sea in rivers. This links which systems?
options: atmospheric and hydrological, with geomorphic effects as rivers erode
ecological and geomorphic only, with no involvement of the atmosphere
hydrological only, because water never leaves the ocean in this cycle
atmospheric only, because rainfall is not part of the water cycle
questions.explanation: Evaporation, condensation and precipitation are atmospheric processes in the water cycle, and runoff in rivers erodes and transports sediment, a geomorphic process. Natural systems are interconnected.

questions.stem: Which process breaks down rocks in place, without moving the fragments?
options: deposition
transportation
weathering
erosion
questions.explanation: Weathering breaks rock down where it is by physical, chemical or biological processes. Erosion and transportation move the material, and deposition lays it down.

questions.stem: Mountain ranges such as the Himalaya are rising where tectonic plates:
options: slide past each other along a transform plate boundary
sink together into the mantle beneath a stable continent
converge, as the Indian Plate pushes into Eurasia
diverge, as new crust forms along a mid-ocean ridge
questions.explanation: The collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates has folded and uplifted crust to form the Himalaya. Divergent boundaries form rift valleys and ridges, and transform boundaries cause earthquakes.

questions.stem: In a hot, humid climate, granite weathers deeply into clay, while in a cold climate it shatters into angular blocks through freeze-thaw. This shows that:
options: rock type is the only factor that controls how rocks are weathered
chemical weathering is fastest where temperatures stay below freezing
weathering does not occur in any climate where rainfall is high
climate, an atmospheric factor, shapes geomorphic processes
questions.explanation: Warmth and moisture speed chemical weathering, while repeated freezing and thawing of water in cracks drives physical weathering. The atmosphere thus shapes geomorphic processes.

questions.stem: In an ecosystem, organisms that break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil are called:
options: top predators
decomposers
producers
primary consumers
questions.explanation: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria recycle nutrients from dead organisms and wastes so that producers can use them again. Producers make food by photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how energy and nutrients move through an ecosystem?
options: nutrients flow through it once; energy cycles repeatedly
both energy and nutrients cycle repeatedly without any loss
both energy and nutrients enter only from groundwater
energy flows through it once; nutrients cycle repeatedly
questions.explanation: Solar energy is captured by producers and lost as heat at each trophic level, so it must be continually replaced. Nutrients are recycled by decomposition.

questions.stem: About what share of the Earth's surface is covered by water?
options: about 29%
about 50%
about 90%
about 71%
questions.explanation: Oceans and seas cover about 71% of the Earth's surface and land about 29%. Much of the land is itself covered by ice, desert, forest, grassland or farmland.

questions.stem: Which list correctly gives major types of land cover on Earth?
options: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere
primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary industry
forest, grassland, desert, ice, wetland and cropland
igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock layers
questions.explanation: Land cover is the physical material on the surface. The other lists describe rock types, layers of the atmosphere and economic sectors.

questions.stem: Over the past million years, Earth has alternated between glacial and interglacial periods. These cycles are mainly paced by:
options: changes in the number of people living on Earth at each stage
the drift of continents across the equator every few thousand years
regular changes in Earth's orbit and tilt (Milankovitch cycles)
the eruption of a single volcano at the start of each glacial period
questions.explanation: Variations in the shape of Earth's orbit, the tilt of its axis and the timing of the seasons change how sunlight is distributed. Feedbacks such as ice albedo and carbon dioxide then amplify the change.

questions.stem: During the last glacial period, sea level was much lower than today and Tasmania was joined to mainland Australia by land across what is now Bass Strait. This shows how glacial cycles change:
options: the composition of the oceans from salt water to fresh water
the length of the day through changes in Earth's rotation
the pattern of land and water through sea level change
the position of the continents through rapid tectonic movement
questions.explanation: As ice sheets grew on land, sea level fell and continental shelves were exposed, joining land masses. As ice melted, rising seas flooded these areas. Continents did not move noticeably in that time.

questions.stem: As ice sheets expand, more sunlight is reflected, the planet cools further and more ice forms. This process is an example of:
options: an output of matter from the hydrological system to space
a positive feedback that amplifies the initial change
a negative feedback that returns the system to balance
a store that removes energy permanently from the system
questions.explanation: The ice-albedo feedback reinforces cooling during glacial periods and warming as ice retreats. Negative feedbacks would counteract the change.

questions.stem: Which evidence allows scientists to reconstruct past climatic and glacial cycles over hundreds of thousands of years?
options: satellite images taken since the 1970s
the dates of recorded volcanic eruptions
air bubbles and isotopes in ice cores
daily weather records kept since the 1700s
questions.explanation: Ice cores from Antarctica contain trapped air and isotopes that record temperature and greenhouse gas levels over about 800 000 years. Instrument records and satellites cover only recent centuries or decades.

questions.stem: Ecological succession is:
options: the clearing of vegetation by people for agriculture
the gradual change in a community's species over time
the sudden extinction of all species in an ecosystem
the movement of animals between seasons to find food
questions.explanation: Succession is the sequence of communities that develops on a site over time, from pioneer species towards a more stable, complex community. Migration and clearing are different processes.

questions.stem: After the 1883 eruption of Krakatau sterilised the island, plants and animals gradually recolonised the bare volcanic surface. This is an example of:
options: primary succession on newly exposed surfaces
secondary succession on soil left after a fire
a climax community that never changes again
deforestation caused by human land clearing
questions.explanation: Primary succession begins on surfaces with no soil, such as new lava or ash, where pioneer species like lichens, mosses and grasses colonise first. Secondary succession follows disturbance where soil remains.

questions.stem: After a bushfire burns a eucalypt forest, grasses and shrubs sprout from the soil and the forest gradually regrows. This is:
options: glaciation
desertification
secondary succession
primary succession
questions.explanation: Secondary succession occurs where soil and seeds remain after a disturbance such as fire or flood, so recovery is much faster than primary succession. Many Australian plants resprout or germinate after fire.

questions.stem: The first species to colonise a bare surface, such as lichens on new rock, are called:
options: pioneer species
climax species
keystone predators
invasive pests
questions.explanation: Pioneer species tolerate harsh conditions and begin forming soil and shelter, making it possible for other species to establish. Climax species dominate a mature community.

questions.stem: Over thousands of years after the last glacial period, forests advanced into areas that had been tundra or grassland as temperatures rose. This change in land cover resulted mainly from:
options: a fall in sea level that drained former oceans
increased glaciation over the newly forested land
natural invasion of vegetation as climate warmed
planting of forests by early farming societies
questions.explanation: As the climate warmed, trees spread (invaded) into newly suitable areas, and succession replaced earlier communities. This is a natural process linking climatic cycles to vegetation change.

questions.stem: Mount Kosciuszko, mainland Australia's highest peak, rises to about:
questions.explanation: Mount Kosciuszko is 2 228 m high, in the Snowy Mountains of NSW. Australia's mountains are low by world standards because they are old and heavily eroded.

questions.stem: Blue Lake, Lake Cootapatamba and Club Lake on the Kosciuszko Main Range occupy hollows carved by ice. These lakes are evidence that:
options: the lakes were dug by people to store water for farming
small glaciers formed there during the last glacial period
the area was covered by the sea until about 1000 years ago
a large volcano erupted there in the last few centuries
questions.explanation: The Main Range holds mainland Australia's only glacial lakes, in cirques and behind moraines left by small glaciers during the last glacial period. They show how climatic cycles shaped this place.

questions.stem: A cirque, such as the hollow holding Blue Lake, is best described as:
options: an armchair-shaped hollow eroded by a glacier at its head
a ridge of rock debris dumped at the snout of a glacier
a long, narrow inlet of the sea in a drowned glacial valley
a cone of ash and lava built up around a volcanic vent
questions.explanation: Cirques form where snow accumulates and ice erodes the slope by plucking and abrasion. A moraine is a ridge of glacial debris, and a fjord is a drowned glacial valley.

questions.stem: Today, freeze-thaw and frost heave still shape soils and slopes in the Kosciuszko alpine area. Processes like these, in cold environments without glaciers, are called:
options: volcanic processes
coastal processes
periglacial processes
tropical processes
questions.explanation: Periglacial processes, such as frost shattering and frost heave, act in cold climates around or after glaciers. They produce features such as stone stripes and solifluction terraces.

questions.stem: Alpine plants above the treeline in the Kosciuszko area are adapted to snow cover for several months each year. If warming shortens the snow season, which natural process is most likely?
options: succession stops completely because plants cannot grow
shrubs and trees invade higher, displacing alpine herbfields
the treeline moves downhill as glaciers return to the range
alpine herbfields spread lower as summers become cooler
questions.explanation: Snow cover and cold limit where trees and shrubs can grow. As conditions warm, woody plants can invade upslope, shrinking the specialised alpine communities that have nowhere higher to go.

questions.stem: The Snowy Mountains, which include the Kosciuszko alpine area, are the source of the Murray, Murrumbidgee and Snowy rivers. In terms of natural systems, this shows the region's role in:
options: the atmospheric system, generating tropical cyclones each summer
the ecological system, supporting coral reefs in its lakes
the hydrological system, storing snow that feeds rivers
the geomorphic system, producing lava flows that block valleys
questions.explanation: Winter snow is a natural store that melts in spring, feeding major rivers and wetlands downstream. This links the alpine area to distant places across south-eastern Australia.

questions.stem: Which combination of natural processes has most shaped the land and water cover of the Kosciuszko alpine area?
options: recent volcanic eruptions, coral reef growth and coastal wave erosion
tropical monsoon rain, desert dune formation and mangrove expansion
tectonic uplift in the last century and the formation of new glaciers
past glaciation, periglacial activity, snow cover and succession
questions.explanation: Small glaciers carved cirques and lakes in the last glacial period, cold-climate processes continue to shape soils, and seasonal snow controls the distribution of alpine plant communities.
